Suddenly
sŭd´n-lĭ
adv. (without warning, in a moment; rendering Hebrew pith'om, Greek exaiphnēs, aphnō)
From Latin subitaneus, from subire, to come up stealthily. Scripture uses it for the two great unannounced arrivals — the Spirit's and the Judge's.

Biblical Definition

Suddenly in Scripture is the adverb of divine arrival, and it cuts two ways. Malachi promises it of the Messiah: “the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in” (Mal 3:1) — long-awaited and yet, when He came, unannounced and unrecognised by the very courts that kept His feasts. Luke records it of the Spirit: “And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting” (Act 2:2). For the disobedient the same adverb is terror: “Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy” (Pro 6:15). And our Lord makes it the ground of the standing command to watch: “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” (Mar 13:36). The suddenness is not God's carelessness about warning; He has warned for centuries. It is the mercy of a fixed hour withheld, so that His servants are kept awake and His enemies are never able to time their repentance for the last safe moment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines suddenly as in an unexpected manner, without warning or previous notice, and hastily, without premeditation.

expand to see more

SUDDENLY, adv. In an unexpected manner; unexpectedly; hastily; without preparation.

2. Without premeditation.

SUDDEN, a. Happening without previous notice; coming unexpectedly, or without the common preparatives.

Key Scripture

Mal 3:1 — "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts."

Act 2:2 — "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting."

Pro 6:15 — "Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy."

Mar 13:36 — "Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping."

Modern Corruption

Suddenness has been shifted from the Judge to the calendar — date-setting on one side, and on the other the assumption that the world will simply go on, so that the one command attached to the word (watch) is the one thing not done.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors both silence the adverb. The date-setters, from the Millerites to every chart-drawing successor, treat the hour as calculable, which is a flat contradiction of the Lord who said no man knoweth the day nor the hour; each failed date leaves the church more cynical about the coming itself. The practical scoffers of 2 Peter 3 take the other road: all things continue as they were from the beginning, and therefore nothing will suddenly change. The first makes the coming a puzzle; the second makes it a rumour.

The biblical response is neither computation nor complacency but watchfulness — a settled readiness that makes the hour irrelevant. “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” is the Lord's own application, and it is addressed to servants with work in their hands, not to speculators with charts. Malachi's warning stands over the religious in particular: the temple was busy the day He arrived, and busyness was no protection at all.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pith'om (H6597), suddenly, in an instant; Greek exaiphnēs (G1810) and aphnō (G869), suddenly — the Spirit's descent and the Judge's arrival.

expand to see more

Hebrew pith'om (H6597) — suddenly, unexpectedly; the calamity of Pro 6:15 and the LORD's coming to His temple (Mal 3:1).

Greek aphnō (G869) — suddenly; the sound from heaven at Pentecost (Act 2:2).

Greek exaiphnēs (G1810) — on a sudden; “lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” (Mar 13:36).

Usage

"“The Lord… shall suddenly come to his temple” — long promised, and still unlooked for."

"“Suddenly there came a sound from heaven” — the Spirit given without a countdown."

"“Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping” — the command that the adverb exists to enforce."
